docs.text:
Fluent Data Toolkit for Jakarta EE / CDI

A lightweight, modular toolkit for data access, messaging, and application infrastructure — built on standard Jakarta EE and CDI.

Get Started GitHub

docs.title: What is FluDa?
docs.text:
FluDa provides a developer-friendly, fluent programming model for data access that mirrors modern APIs like Spring's JdbcClient — without the bulk of a full framework. It is organized into seven standalone pillars:

  • JDBC Client

    A lightweight, type-safe, fluent query engine built directly over JDBC.

    → Getting Started jdbc-client

  • SQL Initialization

    Automates database schema management and data population on application startup.

    → Getting Started sql-init

  • Transaction Support

    Container-agnostic declarative and programmatic transaction boundaries.

    → Getting Started tx

  • Mail

    Simple mail abstraction with Jakarta Mail and pluggable providers.

    → Getting Started mail

  • Data

    A Jakarta Data implementation — @Repository interfaces with query-by-method-name, @Find, and @Query, generated at compile time and executed through JdbcClient.

    → Getting Started data

  • JMS Client

    A fluent Jakarta Messaging client with CDI wiring, payload converters and cached connections.

    → Getting Started jms-client

  • Conditional Beans

    A portable CDI extension that enables a bean only when a condition matches the current deployment.

    → Getting Started conditional-beans

docs.title: Why FluDa?
docs.text:
• Lightweight

    Zero framework dependencies — built on standard CDI and Jakarta EE. No Spring, no heavyweight runtime.

  • Modular

    Use only what you need — core, config, CDI, or any combination — across every pillar.

  • Jakarta EE/CDI Friendly

    Built on standard Jakarta EE, CDI, Jakarta Data, and MicroProfile Config. Works with GlassFish, WildFly, and any compatible server.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
Add the dependency to your project:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0-Beta1</version>
</dependency>

Then create a client from any DataSource and run fluent queries:

import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.JdbcClient;

// Create a client from any DataSource
JdbcClient client = new JdbcClient(dataSource);

// Fluent queries with named parameters
List<Engineer> engineers = client.sql("SELECT id, name FROM engineers WHERE department = :dept")
        .param("dept", "Engineering")
        .query(Engineer.class)
        .list();

// Updates with generated keys
int rows = client.sql("INSERT INTO engineers (name, department) VALUES (:name, :dept)")
        .param("name", "Ada Lovelace")
        .param("dept", "Engineering")
        .update();

See the getting started guide for all options.

docs.text: Welcome to the FluDa blog. Here you'll find announcements, tutorials, and deep dives into the toolkit.

docs.title: Introducing Fluda JdbcClient 1.0.0.Beta1
docs.text:
As I mentioned in my LinkedIn posts, the original JdbcClient CDI project has moved to the new FluDaKit community and become an umbrella project with several subprojects. I have made a number of small updates to jdbc-client over the past few weeks. Today I'm excited to announce that JdbcClient 1.0.0.Beta1 is now available from the public Maven repository. If we find no major issues, this will be the only preview before 1.0.0 final.

JdbcClient is a small, fluent JDBC client for Java 21+, Jakarta EE, and CDI applications. It gives you the query and update API you may know from Spring's JdbcClient or JdbcTemplate, without adding a Spring dependency to a standard Jakarta EE project. The core module is built directly on javax.sql.DataSource and has no runtime framework dependency.

docs.title: Why another JDBC client?
docs.text:
Plain JDBC is powerful, but everyday data access often involves a lot of ceremony:

  • Open a Connection.
  • Prepare a statement.
  • Bind parameters by index.
  • Map a ResultSet by hand.
  • Close every resource correctly.

Frameworks solved this years ago. But if your application is built on Jakarta EE and CDI, adding a full Spring stack just for a better JDBC API is a poor trade-off. JPA is a good fit for rich domain models, but it can feel heavy for simple SQL.

JdbcClient is a lightweight alternative that keeps the focus on JDBC:

  • Fluent SQL API — client.sql(...) guides you through parameters, queries, and updates.
  • Named and positional parameters — use :name or ?, with configurable placeholder rewriting for different databases.
  • Typed result mapping — map rows directly to records and POJOs, or supply a RowMapper.
  • Generated key support — retrieve database-generated keys with a GeneratedKeyHolder.
  • Batch updates — send groups of changes as maps or arrays of parameters.
  • CDI integration — add fluda-jdbc-cdi and inject a ready-to-use JdbcClient.
  • No framework lock-in — you provide the DataSource; JdbcClient uses it through standard JDBC.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Make sure you have Java 21+ and Maven 3.9+ installed, then create a new Maven project from IDE or Maven archetype.

mvn archetype:generate \
-DgroupId=com.example \
-DartifactId=jdbc-client-demo \
-DarchetypeArtifactId=maven-archetype-quickstart \
-DinteractiveMode=false

Open your pom.xml, and add the core artifact and a JDBC driver, such as H2:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-core</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0.Beta1</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.h2database</groupId>
    <artifactId>h2</artifactId>
    <version>2.5.252</version>
</dependency>

[!NOTE] We'll cover the fluda-jdbc-cdi module, which provides CDI integration, later in this post. The optional fluda-jdbc-config module reads settings from MicroProfile Config. All JdbcClient modules share the same version.

docs.title: Using JdbcClient
docs.text:
To create a JdbcClient, provide a DataSource and pass it to the constructor:

import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.JdbcClient;
...
var ds = Utils.newDataSource(); // an in-memory H2 DataSource in the example
JdbcClient client = new JdbcClient(ds);

Then use this jdbc client to execute SQL statements. The following example shows how to insert a row and retrieve the generated key, then query all rows and map them to a record:

import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.support.GeneratedKeyHolder;
import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.support.KeyHolder;

import java.util.List;

public record Engineer(Long id, String name) {
}

// Insert and retrieve the generated id.
KeyHolder holder = new GeneratedKeyHolder();
client.sql("INSERT INTO engineers (name) VALUES (:name)")
        .param("name", "Ada")
        .update(holder);

long adaId = ((Number) holder.getKey()).longValue();

// Map rows directly to a record.
List<Engineer> all = client
        .sql("SELECT id, name FROM engineers ORDER BY id")
        .query(Engineer.class)
        .list();

Similar to the previous example, use the same client for reads, updates, and deletes:

Engineer ada = client.sql("SELECT id, name FROM engineers WHERE id = :id")
        .param("id", adaId)
        .query(Engineer.class)
        .single();

client.sql("UPDATE engineers SET name = :name WHERE id = :id")
        .param("name", "Ada Lovelace")
        .param("id", adaId)
        .update();

client.sql("DELETE FROM engineers WHERE id = :id")
        .param("id", adaId)
        .update();

That is the whole model: a JdbcClient instance, a fluent specification, and standard JDBC under the covers.

This example is adapted from VanillaExample in the Fludakit examples repository.

To customize client-wide defaults, create the client with the builder:

JdbcClient client = JdbcClient.builder(dataSource)
        .placeholder("?")
        .queryTimeout(30)
        .fetchSize(100)
        .build();

docs.title: Using JdbcClient with CDI
docs.text:
Add the fluda-jdbc-cdi module to your pom.xml:

<dependency>
    <groupId>io.github.fludakit</groupId>
    <artifactId>fluda-jdbc-cdi</artifactId>
    <version>1.0.0.Beta1</version>
</dependency>

In a CDI environment, this module supplies the JdbcClient producer. Expose a DataSource bean, then inject the client where you need it:

import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.JdbcClient;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.inject.Inject;

@ApplicationScoped
public class EngineerService {

    @Inject
    JdbcClient client;

    public Engineer findById(Long id) {
        return client.sql("SELECT id, name FROM engineers WHERE id = :id")
                .param("id", id)
                .query(Engineer.class)
                .single();
    }
}

Its DataSourceProducer creates a HikariCP pool and exposes it to CDI:

@ApplicationScoped
public class DataSourceProducer {

    private final HikariDataSource raw;

    public DataSourceProducer() {
        HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:h2:mem:javase;DB_CLOSE_DELAY=-1");
        config.setUsername("sa");
        config.setPassword("");
        config.setMaximumPoolSize(10);
        this.raw = new HikariDataSource(config);
    }

    @Produces
    @Singleton
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        return raw;
    }
}

The service code stays the same whether the DataSource comes from a local pool, a servlet container, or a Jakarta EE server.

The javase example uses this pattern and starts CDI with Weld SE.

docs.title: Providing a DataSource in Tomcat
docs.text:
The Tomcat container context manages the connection pools globally. Add a META-INF/context.xml, declare a javax.sql.DataSource resource, which can be accessed via JNDI:

<Context>
    <Resource name="jdbc/myDS"
              auth="Container"
              type="javax.sql.DataSource"
              driverClassName="org.mariadb.jdbc.Driver"
              url="jdbc:mariadb://localhost:3306/servlet"
              username="root"
              password="root"
              maxTotal="8"
              maxIdle="4"/>
</Context>

The following DataSourceProducer obtains the resource with @Resource and republishes it as a CDI bean:

@ApplicationScoped
public class DataSourceProducer {

    @Resource(name = "jdbc/myDS")
    private DataSource dataSource;

    @Produces
    @Singleton
    public DataSource expose() {
        return dataSource;
    }
}

After that, the rest of the application is ordinary JdbcClient code. See the example's EngineerService and EngineerServlet for a compact CRUD flow.

The servlet example runs on Tomcat 11 with Weld Servlet.

docs.title: Providing a DataSource in Jakarta EE
docs.text:
In Jakarta EE, you can create a custom DataSource with the @DataSourceDefinition annotation. The following example declares a PostgreSQL data source under a portable JNDI name, injects it with @Resource, and exposes it as a CDI bean:

import javax.sql.DataSource;
import jakarta.annotation.Resource;
import jakarta.annotation.sql.DataSourceDefinition;
import jakarta.enterprise.context.ApplicationScoped;
import jakarta.enterprise.inject.Produces;

@DataSourceDefinition(
        name = "java:app/MyDS",
        className = "org.postgresql.xa.PGXADataSource",
        url = "jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/testdb",
        user = "testuser",
        password = "testpassword"
)
@ApplicationScoped
public class DataSourceProducer {

    @Resource(lookup = "java:app/MyDS")
    private DataSource dataSource;

    @Produces
    @ApplicationScoped
    public DataSource expose() {
        return dataSource;
    }
}

The jakartaee example targets GlassFish and WildFly. A real deployment can replace the annotation-defined data source with one configured by the application server. The injection point remains @Inject JdbcClient client;, and JdbcClient works with the container-managed connection pool.

Because this is a full Jakarta EE runtime, container-provided @Transactional is available for transaction boundaries. The example does not require an additional FluDa transaction dependency.

For more use cases—generated keys, batch updates, result mapping options, converters, streaming, and configuration—see the reference documentation.

docs.title: Try the examples
docs.text:
The complete runnable examples are in the fludakit/examples repository:

  • vanilla — the core client with no CDI, backed by an in-memory H2 database.
  • javase — CDI with Weld SE and a HikariCP pool.
  • servlet — Tomcat 11, Weld Servlet, and a JNDI DataSource.
  • jakartaee — JAX-RS on GlassFish or WildFly with a container-defined DataSource.

docs.title: What's next
docs.text: 1.0.0.Beta1 is our invitation to try JdbcClient before the final release. If you find a rough edge, have an API suggestion, or want to share how you provide a DataSource in your environment, open an issue on GitHub. Your feedback will help shape 1.0.0 final.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
FluDa (Fluent Data Toolkit for Jakarta EE/CDI) is a lightweight, modular data-access suite designed for standard Jakarta EE and CDI environments. It provides a developer-friendly, fluent programming model that mirrors modern data APIs like Spring's JdbcClient — without requiring Spring or introducing bulky dependencies.

FluDa is organized into seven standalone modules. Each module ships its own reference documentation, published from the module repository:

docs.title: JDBC Client
docs.text:
A lightweight, type-safe, fluent query engine built directly over JDBC. The core module has zero framework dependencies — just JDBC and a DataSource.

  • Fluent API with named and positional parameters
  • POJO mapping with custom row mappers
  • Generated key support
  • CDI integration for dependency injection

Get started with JDBC Client →

docs.title: SQL Initialization
docs.text:
Automates database schema management and data population on application startup. Perfect for development and testing scenarios where you need to set up database state automatically.

  • Schema creation from SQL scripts
  • Data population from SQL files
  • CDI integration for automatic execution

Get started with SQL Init →

docs.title: Transaction Support
docs.text:
Container-agnostic declarative and programmatic transaction boundaries backed directly by a standard DataSource or JPA. Works in Java SE, Servlet containers, and Jakarta EE environments.

  • @Transactional interceptor for CDI beans
  • Resource-local transactions without JTA
  • Transaction propagation control
  • Transaction-phase callbacks and events

Get started with Transaction Support →

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
A simple mail abstraction with built-in Jakarta Mail (SMTP) support and pluggable providers for third-party services like SendGrid.

  • MailSender interface with JakartaMailSender implementation
  • Fluent MailBuilder for composing messages
  • Template support with FreeMarker and simple placeholder processing
  • CDI integration with MicroProfile Config properties
  • Pluggable providers — implement MailSender for any email service

Get started with Mail →

docs.title: Data
docs.text:
A Jakarta Data implementation for Jakarta EE and CDI. You declare a @Repository interface, and an annotation processor generates the implementation at compile time — no runtime proxies, no classpath scanning.

  • Lifecycle annotations (@Insert, @Update, @Save, @Delete)
  • Built-in repository methods, @Find / @By / @OrderBy, and @Query
  • Optional query-by-method-name parser
  • Generated code executes SQL through the FluDa JDBC Client

Get started with Data →

docs.title: JMS Client
docs.text:
A fluent Jakarta Messaging client in the style of Spring's JmsClient, with CDI wiring and MicroProfile Config for Java SE and Jakarta EE.

  • JmsClient with fluent send, receive, receive-selected and browse operations
  • MessageConverter SPI — SimpleMessageConverter by default, optional JSON-B
  • CachingConnectionFactory reuses one JMSContext per thread
  • CDI producers that resolve a JMSContext, a ConnectionFactory or a configured Artemis/Qpid section

Get started with JMS Client →

docs.title: Conditional Beans
docs.text:
A portable CDI extension that enables a bean only when a condition matches the current deployment.

  • @Conditional with repeatable support and stereotype composition
  • Condition and ConditionContext for deployment-time decisions
  • Built-in @ConditionalOnBean, @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnProperty and their missing counterparts
  • Two runtimes — CDI Full (portable extension) and CDI Lite (build compatible extension)

Get started with Conditional Beans →

docs.title: Conditional Beans
docs.text:
A portable CDI extension that enables a bean only when a condition matches the current deployment.

Documentation fludakit.github.io/conditional-beans Source github.com/fludakit/conditional-beans Artifacts fluda-conditional-beans-api, fluda-conditional-beans-full, fluda-conditional-beans-lite

The reference documentation for this module lives in the module repository and is published with GitHub Pages. The extension is registered through META-INF/services/jakarta.enterprise.inject.spi.Extension, so it is active in every deployment that has the artifact on the classpath. When a condition does not match, the bean is vetoed during bootstrap: it is not injectable, it does not show up in BeanManager.getBeans(...), and it produces no ProcessBean event.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
public class ChinaCondition implements Condition<Conditional> {

    @Override
    public boolean matches(ConditionContext context, Conditional annotation) {
        return "CN".equals(context.getProperty("app.country").orElse(null));
    }
}

docs.title: Sections
docs.text: • Getting Started — add the artifact, declare your first condition, and pick the runtime that fits your deployment.

import io.github.fludakit.data.annotation.Entity;

    String title;

docs.title: JDBC Client
docs.text:
A lightweight, type-safe, fluent query engine built directly over JDBC for Jakarta EE / CDI applications.

Documentation fludakit.github.io/jdbc-client Source github.com/fludakit/jdbc-client Artifacts fluda-jdbc-core, fluda-jdbc-config, fluda-jdbc-cdi

The reference documentation for this module lives in the module repository and is published with GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import io.github.fludakit.jdbc.JdbcClient;
import javax.sql.DataSource;

DataSource dataSource = ...; // obtain a DataSource from your application or runtime
JdbcClient client = new JdbcClient(dataSource);

List<Engineer> engineers = client.sql("SELECT id, name FROM engineers WHERE department = :dept")
        .param("dept", "Engineering")
        .query(Engineer.class)
        .list();

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Getting Started — add the dependency, run your first query, and review configuration options such as placeholders, timeouts, and defaults.
  • Querying and Result Mapping — named and positional parameters, POJO mapping, and custom row mappers.
  • Updates and Generated Keys — inserts, updates, batches, and generated key retrieval.

docs.title: JMS Client
docs.text:
A fluent Jakarta Messaging client in the style of Spring's JmsClient, with CDI wiring and MicroProfile Config.

Documentation fludakit.github.io/jms-client Source github.com/fludakit/jms-client Artifacts fluda-jms-core, fluda-jms-config, fluda-jms-cdi, fluda-jms-artemis, fluda-jms-qpid

The reference documentation for this module lives in the module repository and is published with GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import io.github.fludakit.jms.CachingConnectionFactory;
import io.github.fludakit.jms.JmsClient;
import org.apache.activemq.artemis.jms.client.ActiveMQJMSConnectionFactory;

import java.io.Serializable;

record Order(String id, String item, int quantity) implements Serializable {
}

try (var factory = new ActiveMQJMSConnectionFactory("tcp://localhost:61616", "artemis", "artemis");
     var caching = new CachingConnectionFactory(factory)) {

    JmsClient client = JmsClient.builder(caching).build();

    client.destination("orders").send(new Order("order-1", "keyboard", 2));
}

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Getting Started — add the dependency and exchange your first messages.
  • Jakarta EE — using the container-provided JMSContext.
  • Message Converter — the MessageConverter SPI and payload conversion.
  • Destination Resolver — resolving destinations by name.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
A simple mail abstraction with built-in Jakarta Mail (SMTP) support and pluggable providers for third-party services.

Documentation fludakit.github.io/mail Source github.com/fludakit/mail Artifacts fluda-mail-core, fluda-mail-config, fluda-mail-cdi

The reference documentation for this module lives in the module repository and is published with GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import io.github.fludakit.mail.JakartaMailSender;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailMessage;
import io.github.fludakit.mail.MailSender;

import jakarta.mail.Session;
import java.util.Properties;

Properties props = new Properties();
props.put("mail.smtp.host", "smtp.example.com");
props.put("mail.smtp.port", "587");
props.put("mail.smtp.auth", "true");
props.put("mail.smtp.starttls.enable", "true");

Session session = Session.getInstance(props);
MailSender sender = new JakartaMailSender(session);

MailMessage message = new MailMessage();
message.setFrom("sender@example.com");
message.addTo("recipient@example.com");
message.setSubject("Hello from FluDa Mail");
message.setHtmlBody("<p>This is a test email sent with FluDa Mail.</p>");
sender.send(message);

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Getting Started — add dependencies and send your first email.
  • Mail Sender — the MailSender abstraction and the built-in Jakarta Mail implementation.
  • Template Resolver — rendering email templates with FreeMarker or simple placeholder processing.

docs.title: Transaction Support
docs.text:
Container-agnostic declarative and programmatic transaction boundaries backed directly by a standard DataSource or JPA.

Documentation fludakit.github.io/tx Source github.com/fludakit/tx Artifacts fluda-tx-core, fluda-tx-cdi, fluda-tx-jdbc, fluda-tx-jpa

The reference documentation for this module lives in the module repository and is published with GitHub Pages.

docs.title: Quick example
docs.text:
import io.github.fludakit.tx.PlatformTransactionManager;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.jdbc.DataSourceTransactionManager;
import io.github.fludakit.tx.jdbc.TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy;

import javax.sql.DataSource;

DataSource pool = ...; // your raw pool
TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy dataSource = new TransactionAwareDataSourceProxy(pool);
PlatformTransactionManager transactionManager = new DataSourceTransactionManager(pool);

docs.title: Sections
docs.text:
• Getting Started — add dependencies and set up resource-local transactions in a CDI environment.
  • JDBC Implementation — resource-local transactions over a plain DataSource.
  • JPA Implementation — transactions driven by an EntityManager.
  • Mixing JDBC and JPA — multiple data sources and sharing one transaction between JPA and JDBC.
